title: GCSE Geography
intro: Plates, storms, rainforests, rivers, coasts and cities: put your GCSE Geography knowledge to the test.

questions.prompt: At which type of plate margin do two plates move apart from each other?
questions.explanation: At constructive margins magma rises to fill the gap as the plates move apart, forming new crust.

questions.prompt: At which type of plate margin do two plates slide past each other without crust being made or destroyed?
questions.explanation: Conservative margins, such as the San Andreas Fault, cause earthquakes but not volcanoes.

questions.prompt: What is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake called?
questions.explanation: The focus is where the earthquake starts underground. The epicentre is directly above it, where shaking is usually strongest.

questions.prompt: A series of large sea waves caused by an undersea earthquake is called a…
questions.explanation: When the sea bed moves suddenly, it pushes up the water above, sending powerful waves across the ocean.

questions.prompt: In the traditional GCSE explanation, convection currents in which layer of the Earth move the tectonic plates?
questions.explanation: Heat from the core warms the mantle, creating slow currents that drag the plates above them.

questions.prompt: What is the calm, clear area at the centre of a tropical storm called?
questions.explanation: The eye has light winds and clear skies, surrounded by the eyewall where the strongest winds blow.

questions.prompt: What is a large ecosystem, such as tropical rainforest or hot desert, that covers a wide area of the world called?
questions.explanation: Biomes are global-scale ecosystems shaped mainly by climate.

questions.prompt: In a tropical rainforest, what is the layer formed by the tallest trees that rise above the canopy called?
questions.explanation: Emergent trees can grow to around 50 metres tall, poking out above the dense canopy.

questions.prompt: What are the large roots that spread out above ground to support tall rainforest trees called?
questions.explanation: Rainforest soils are thin, so buttress roots help hold up very tall trees.

questions.prompt: What is the name for ground that stays frozen all year round in cold environments such as the tundra?
questions.explanation: Permafrost has stayed frozen for at least two years in a row. Only the top layer may thaw in summer.

questions.prompt: Which type of river erosion happens when rocks carried by the river grind against the bed and banks?
questions.explanation: Abrasion works like sandpaper, wearing away the river bed and banks.

questions.prompt: Which erosion process makes rocks smaller and rounder as they knock into each other in the river?
questions.explanation: Attrition explains why stones further downstream are usually smaller and more rounded.

questions.prompt: Which river landform is created when the neck of a meander is cut through and the old loop is left behind?
questions.explanation: Erosion narrows the meander neck until the river breaks through. Deposition then seals off the old loop.

questions.prompt: What is the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries called?
questions.explanation: A drainage basin is separated from the next one by high land called the watershed.

questions.prompt: Which graph shows how a river's discharge changes after a period of rainfall?
questions.explanation: A storm hydrograph shows rainfall and discharge over time, including lag time and peak discharge.

questions.prompt: What is the zigzag movement of sediment along a coastline called?
questions.explanation: Waves arrive at an angle with the prevailing wind, but the backwash runs straight back down the beach, moving sediment along.

questions.prompt: Which landform is a narrow ridge of sand or shingle that sticks out from the coast into the sea?
questions.explanation: Spits form where the coastline changes direction and longshore drift keeps depositing sediment.

questions.prompt: Which hard engineering structure is a low wooden or stone barrier built out across a beach to trap sediment?
questions.explanation: Groynes stop longshore drift carrying the beach away, though they can starve beaches further along the coast.

questions.prompt: Along a headland, erosion can form a crack, a cave and then an arch. What forms when the arch collapses?
questions.explanation: When the arch roof collapses, a stack of rock is left standing alone. Further erosion turns it into a stump.

questions.prompt: What is the increase in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities called?
questions.explanation: Urbanisation is happening fastest in lower income countries, driven by migration and natural increase.

questions.prompt: A city with a population of more than 10 million people is called a…
questions.explanation: Examples of megacities include Lagos, Mumbai and São Paulo.

questions.prompt: When an area's demand for water is greater than its supply, it is said to have a water…
questions.explanation: Much of south-east England has a water deficit, while parts of north and west Britain have a surplus.

questions.prompt: What is the term for the distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten?
questions.explanation: More food miles usually mean more transport emissions, which is one reason people buy local food.

questions.prompt: Composite volcanoes are usually found at destructive plate margins.
questions.explanation: At destructive margins, sticky magma builds steep-sided composite volcanoes from layers of ash and lava.

questions.prompt: Beach nourishment is an example of hard engineering.
questions.explanation: Beach nourishment, adding sand or shingle to a beach, is soft engineering because it works with natural processes.

questions.prompt: The tundra has a long growing season for plants.
questions.explanation: The tundra's growing season is very short, often only around two months, because it is cold for most of the year.

questions.prompt: A brownfield site is land that has been built on before.
questions.explanation: Brownfield sites are previously developed land, often old industrial areas, which can be cleaned up and reused.

questions.prompt: Tropical storms usually need a sea surface temperature of at least about how many degrees Celsius to form?
questions.explanation: Warm oceans of about 27°C or more provide the heat and moisture that power tropical storms.

questions.prompt: What is the highest category on the Saffir-Simpson scale for hurricanes?
questions.explanation: The Saffir-Simpson scale runs from category 1 to category 5, the strongest, based on wind speed.

questions.prompt: The Hadley cell of the global atmospheric circulation stretches from the equator to about which latitude?
questions.explanation: Air rises at the equator, moves towards the poles and sinks at about 30° north and south, creating high pressure.
